front: How does the typical HPV-positive oropharynx cancer patient differ from the HPV-negative patient, and whose prognosis is better?
back: HPV-positive patients are younger and light or never smokers; HPV-negative patients are older heavy smokers and drinkers. HPV-positive disease has the better prognosis, stage for stage.
extra: Because of this, AJCC 8 stages p16-positive and p16-negative oropharynx cancer as two separate diseases.

front: What are the classic risk factors for oral cavity cancer?
back: Tobacco, alcohol, and betel nut (areca) chewing
extra: It often starts as leukoplakia. Any nonhealing white or red oral lesion gets a biopsy.

front: Which virus drives nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and where is the disease endemic?
back: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV); endemic in southern China, Southeast Asia, and North Africa
extra: Salt-preserved fish is the classic dietary risk factor. Endemic disease is the nonkeratinizing, undifferentiated type with the best prognosis. Plasma EBV DNA is used for prognosis and response monitoring in NPC.

front: Why is p16 staining used as the test for HPV in oropharynx cancer?
back: High-risk HPV's E7 protein inactivates pRb, which normally keeps p16 turned down, so p16 becomes overexpressed and shows up on a simple immunostain.
extra: HPV-negative tumors are driven by p53 mutation instead.

front: Does p16 positivity change the staging of an oral tongue cancer?
back: No. p16 only counts in the oropharynx (and unknown primaries with a neck node). A p16-positive oral tongue cancer is staged as oral cavity.
extra: Always identify the subsite before choosing the staging system.

front: Which oral lesions are premalignant, and how should a nonhealing one be handled?
back: Leukoplakia (white patch) and erythroplakia (red patch). Any nonhealing white or red lesion gets a biopsy, not reassurance.
extra: Field cancerization in smokers means second primaries happen, so examine the whole mouth.

front: What blood test is used as a tumor marker in nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
back: Plasma EBV DNA, for staging and for following response
extra: EBER testing on the biopsy confirms EBV-related tumor.

front: Which landmark divides the oral tongue from the base of tongue, and why does that line matter?
back: The circumvallate papillae. In front is oral tongue (oral cavity, treated with surgery first); behind is base of tongue (oropharynx, often HPV-driven and often treated with radiation).
extra: Same organ, two different diseases with different staging and treatment.

front: Which two oropharynx subsites are where HPV-positive cancers classically start?
back: The palatine tonsil and the base of tongue
extra: The other two oropharynx subsites are the soft palate and posterior pharyngeal wall. Base of tongue primaries can be tiny and hidden behind a big neck node.

front: Why does an adult with a new one-sided serous otitis media need the nasopharynx examined?
back: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma usually starts in the fossa of Rosenmüller, right beside the eustachian tube opening, and can block the tube.
extra: Scope the nasopharynx. Other NPC presentations: neck mass (most common), nasal obstruction or epistaxis, and cranial nerve palsies.

front: Which cranial nerve is most often affected when nasopharyngeal carcinoma invades the skull base, and what does any cranial nerve palsy do to the T stage?
back: CN VI (abducens), causing diplopia. Any cranial nerve involvement makes it T4.
extra: The neuro exam is part of staging in the nasopharynx.

front: Which laryngeal compartment has almost no lymphatics, and what does that mean for treatment?
back: The glottis (true vocal cords). Early glottic cancer is treated without covering the neck.
extra: Early glottic nodal risk is only about 2-5%. The supraglottis drains richly to both sides of the neck, so supraglottic cancer gets bilateral neck coverage.

front: A smoker has ear pain but a normal ear exam. What should you suspect?
back: Referred otalgia from a pharyngeal or laryngeal cancer
extra: Tonsil and base of tongue refer pain through CN IX (Jacobson's nerve); larynx and hypopharynx through CN X (Arnold's nerve).

front: What does new trismus suggest in an oral cavity or oropharynx cancer?
back: Spread into the pterygoid muscles / masticator space, which means very advanced (T4) disease
extra: Masticator space invasion is T4b (generally unresectable) in the oral cavity. Retromolar trigone tumors reach the pterygoids early.

front: Which oral cavity subsite sits right on bone and invades the mandible early?
back: The gingiva (alveolar ridge)
extra: Bone invasion is T4a only if it goes through cortical bone, not superficial erosion of a tooth socket.

front: A patient with oral tongue cancer has a numb anterior tongue. What does that suggest, and what should you order?
back: Perineural invasion along the lingual nerve (CN V3). Get an MRI for perineural spread.
extra: PNI can track back toward the foramen ovale and skull base, so the radiation field may follow the nerve.

front: Ear pain with a normal ear exam in a tonsil cancer is referred along which nerve?
back: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), which supplies both the tonsil and the middle ear
extra: In supraglottic or hypopharyngeal cancer, referred otalgia travels along the vagus (CN X).

front: Which cranial nerves are at risk when nasopharyngeal carcinoma spreads back into the parapharyngeal (retrostyloid) space?
back: CN IX, X, XI, XII and the sympathetic chain: hoarseness, dysphagia, shoulder weakness, tongue deviation, and Horner syndrome
extra: Spread up into the cavernous sinus threatens CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI.

front: What are the three compartments of the larynx, and which presents earliest?
back: Supraglottis, glottis, and subglottis. Glottic cancer presents earliest, with hoarseness.
extra: Supraglottic cancer presents late with dysphagia or a neck mass. Subglottic cancer causes stridor.

front: What does a fixed vocal cord do to the T stage of a larynx cancer?
back: Makes it T3
extra: Impaired (not fixed) cord mobility is T2. Paraglottic or pre-epiglottic space invasion is also T3.

front: Which neck nerve crosses levels IIb and V, and what does its injury cause?
back: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI): shoulder drop, weak abduction, and winged scapula
extra: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) crosses level II above the carotid bifurcation; injury makes the tongue deviate toward the injured side.

front: Which landmarks divide neck levels II, III, and IV?
back: The hyoid separates II from III, and the cricoid separates III from IV (the clavicle is the bottom of IV).
extra: Two bones and one cartilage divide the jugular chain.

front: Which neck level is the most commonly involved in head and neck cancer?
back: Level II (upper jugular)
extra: Levels II-IV are common parts of elective neck treatment, but the exact levels and whether one or both sides are treated depend on the primary site and its extent.

front: Which primaries need the retropharyngeal nodes (level VII) covered, and why are these nodes easy to forget?
back: Any pharyngeal primary (nasopharynx, oropharynx, hypopharynx). They are deep and cannot be felt on exam.
extra: Retropharyngeal nodes are the first echelon for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

front: Which head and neck site routinely adds level V (posterior triangle) to the elective neck?
back: Nasopharynx
extra: Other add-ons: subglottic extension → level VI; lower lip, anterior tongue, or anterior floor of mouth → level Ia.

front: When can only one side of the neck be treated in head and neck cancer?
back: For a well-lateralized primary that drains to one side, classically a tonsil cancer without base of tongue or soft palate involvement
extra: Midline or near-midline primaries (base of tongue, soft palate, pharyngeal wall, supraglottis, nasopharynx) get both sides.

front: In head and neck RT, how is a grossly involved node (GTVn) treated differently from an elective nodal level?
back: The involved node gets the full definitive dose; elective levels at risk only for microscopic disease get a lower dose.
extra: The PTV adds a small margin around the CTVs for daily setup variation.

front: Which neck level contains the Delphian node, and when is it covered?
back: Level VI (central compartment). It is covered when there is subglottic extension.
extra: Level VI runs from the hyoid to the sternal notch, between the carotids.

front: Which primaries drain to level Ia (submental)?
back: The lower lip, anterior oral tongue, and anterior floor of mouth
extra: Level Ib (submandibular) is at risk from most oral cavity sites. The hard palate drains to II-IV, not level I.

front: What is the usual nodal drainage order for oral cavity cancer?
back: Level I, then II, then III
extra: Oropharynx follows II, III, IV plus the retropharyngeal nodes. Nasopharynx goes to the retropharyngeal nodes, II, and V on both sides.

front: Which head and neck primaries usually need both sides of the neck treated?
back: Midline or near-midline primaries: base of tongue, soft palate, posterior pharyngeal wall, supraglottis, and nasopharynx, plus any patient with bilateral nodes
extra: A well-lateralized tonsil or oral cavity cancer can often be treated to one side.

front: About what dose do elective neck levels receive compared with gross disease?
back: About 50-56 Gy for elective levels, compared with about 70 Gy to gross disease
extra: Microscopic disease takes less dose to control.

front: Why is CT, rather than MRI, the standard for staging larynx cancer?
back: Cartilage invasion defines the T stage in the larynx, and CT is best for bone and cartilage erosion.
extra: On CT, cartilage invasion shows as sclerosis and cortical erosion.

front: When is MRI the preferred imaging test in head and neck cancer?
back: When soft-tissue extent, perineural spread, or skull base invasion matters, especially for the nasopharynx and for oral cavity depth of invasion
extra: CT is still better for mandible cortex erosion.

front: What are the two main jobs of PET-CT in head and neck cancer?
back: Staging nodes and distant disease (stage III-IV), and after treatment, telling recurrent tumor (FDG-avid) from scar and inflammation
extra: Post-treatment PET is a decision point: a negative scan can spare a neck dissection.

front: What imaging features make a cervical lymph node suspicious for cancer?
back: Short axis >10 mm, loss of the fatty hilum, or cystic/necrotic change
extra: Extranodal extension looks like an ill-defined margin, irregular capsular enhancement, or lost surrounding fat.

front: An adult has a cystic level II neck node and no obvious primary. What diagnosis must be ruled out?
back: HPV-positive oropharynx cancer (often a small or hidden tonsil or base of tongue primary)
extra: Do not call a cystic neck node in an adult a benign branchial cleft cyst until this is excluded.

front: What is the earliest imaging sign of nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
back: Effacement (filling in) of the fossa of Rosenmüller
extra: MRI is the study of choice for skull base, cavernous sinus, and perineural extension.

front: Why is MRI preferred over CT for staging the oral cavity primary?
back: Depth of invasion, the biggest driver of oral cavity T stage, is a soft-tissue measurement.
extra: CT is better for cortical erosion of the mandible.

front: When is PET/CT done after head and neck chemoradiation, and what can a negative scan spare?
back: About 12 weeks after treatment. A negative scan can spare a planned neck dissection.
extra: Active tumor is FDG-avid, while scar usually is not.

front: What MRI signs suggest perineural spread?
back: Nerve thickening, foraminal widening, loss of perineural fat, and abnormal nerve enhancement
extra: Perineural spread is visible on imaging, unlike microscopic perineural invasion seen only on pathology. It most often follows CN V and VII.

front: Which imaging findings suggest extranodal extension, and can imaging confirm it?
back: Loss of the fat plane around the node, irregular capsular enhancement, and ill-defined margins. Only pathology confirms it.
extra: ENE on pathology is one of the two indications for postoperative chemoradiation.

front: Why does every head and neck radiation patient get a dental evaluation before treatment?
back: To extract unhealthy teeth before RT and prevent osteoradionecrosis of the jaw
extra: Patients also get fluoride trays for life, because radiation-induced dry mouth causes aggressive dental decay.

front: Which test must be done on every oropharynx squamous cell carcinoma before it can be staged?
back: p16 immunohistochemistry (the surrogate for HPV)
extra: A neck node FNA usually provides enough tissue. p16 status picks which staging system to use. Why p16 works as a surrogate: the HPV E7 protein inactivates pRb, which normally keeps p16 turned down (E6 degrades p53).

front: In head and neck staging, what is the general difference between T4a and T4b?
back: T4a invades nearby structures but is still resectable; T4b is very advanced and generally unresectable.
extra: T4b examples: carotid encasement, prevertebral space, skull base, masticator space, mediastinum.

front: For non-HPV head and neck cancer, what is the basic difference between N1, N2, and N3?
back: N1 = a single ipsilateral node ≤3 cm. N2 = larger (3-6 cm), multiple, or bilateral/contralateral nodes. N3 = any node >6 cm or clinically obvious extranodal extension.
extra: Applies to oral cavity, larynx, hypopharynx, and p16-negative oropharynx. The N2a/b/c subdivisions are in the staging tables.

front: What feature is built into the T stage of oral cavity cancer but no other head and neck site?
back: Depth of invasion (DOI), with cutoffs at 5 mm and 10 mm
extra: A small but deep tumor can outstage a larger, superficial one.

front: How does p16-positive status change the staging of oropharynx cancer?
back: It uses its own, more favorable AJCC system, so the same tumor gets a lower stage (e.g., any number of ipsilateral nodes ≤6 cm is still N1).
extra: Example: 2.5 cm tonsil primary with three ipsilateral nodes is Stage I if p16+ but Stage IVA if p16-. A lower stage does not mean less treatment off trial.

front: How is N stage determined in nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
back: By side and height, not number: unilateral neck nodes = N1, bilateral = N2, and any node >6 cm or below the cricoid = N3
extra: Nasopharynx T stage also follows where the tumor spread (soft tissue → bone → intracranial/cranial nerves), not its size.

front: In larynx cancer, what makes a tumor T3 vs T4a?
back: T3 = a fixed vocal cord (or paraglottic/pre-epiglottic space or inner thyroid cartilage invasion). T4a = through the outer thyroid cartilage or outside the larynx.
extra: Cord mobility is checked on scope; cartilage invasion is judged on CT.

front: What extra workup does a nasopharyngeal carcinoma need?
back: Nasopharyngoscopy with biopsy (with EBV/EBER testing), MRI of the skull base, and plasma EBV DNA
extra: A larynx or hypopharynx cancer instead adds direct laryngoscopy under anesthesia to assess cord mobility and the airway.

front: What does T0 mean in p16-positive oropharynx cancer?
back: A p16-positive neck node with no primary found
extra: In the nasopharynx, T0 means an EBV-positive neck node with no primary found.

front: How is pathologic N stage assigned for p16-positive oropharynx cancer after surgery?
back: By node count: 1-4 positive nodes = pN1, 5 or more = pN2
extra: Clinical N uses laterality and the 6 cm cutoff. ENE is not used in the p16-positive system.

front: How does microscopic ENE found after surgery change the N stage in non-HPV head and neck cancer?
back: It shifts N up: a single ipsilateral node ≤3 cm with ENE becomes pN2a, and larger, multiple, or contralateral nodes with ENE become pN3b.
extra: Whatever the stage, ENE on pathology means adding chemo to postoperative radiation.

front: Which head and neck site has the worst prognosis, and why?
back: The hypopharynx, because it presents late, usually with nodes
extra: It follows the same larynx-preservation logic as the larynx.

front: What is the primary treatment for resectable oral cavity cancer?
back: Surgery first: resection with negative margins plus a neck dissection (even for a clinically negative neck)
extra: Adjuvant RT ± chemo follows based on pathology. Radiation alone does poorly here and risks osteoradionecrosis.

front: After head and neck cancer surgery, which pathologic findings call for adjuvant radiation?
back: Advanced pathologic stage (pT3-T4 or pN2-N3) or adverse features such as perineural invasion, lymphovascular invasion, or close margins
extra: These predict local and regional recurrence with surgery alone. Postoperative RT is about 60 Gy; ENE or a positive margin adds concurrent cisplatin.

front: Which two pathologic features mean concurrent chemo should be added to postoperative radiation?
back: Extranodal extension (ENE) and a positive margin
extra: From the pooled RTOG 9501 / EORTC 22931 analysis: these were the only features where chemo clearly helped.

front: What is the standard definitive radiation dose for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma?
back: 70 Gy in 35 fractions to gross disease
extra: Lower doses go to at-risk areas, often in the same plan (simultaneous integrated boost). Avoid treatment breaks: tumor repopulation during gaps lowers cure rates, so nutrition and pain are managed proactively.

front: What is the standard postoperative radiation dose for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma?
back: 60 Gy in 30 fractions
extra: Boosted toward 66 Gy for a positive margin or ENE.

front: What is the standard concurrent chemotherapy given with head and neck radiation?
back: Cisplatin
extra: Weekly or every 3 weeks. If cisplatin cannot be given: carboplatin/paclitaxel or cetuximab.

front: Does HPV-positive oropharynx cancer get less intense treatment off trial?
back: No. HPV changes the prognosis, not the treatment; de-escalation is only done on clinical trials.
extra: RTOG 1016 and De-ESCALaTE: swapping cisplatin for cetuximab gave worse survival without meaningfully less toxicity.

front: What are the two main options for early oropharynx cancer, and what should the team try to avoid?
back: Transoral robotic surgery (TORS) or definitive radiation, with similar cure rates. Pick one approach to avoid triple therapy (surgery + RT + chemo).
extra: If surgery is likely to need adjuvant chemoRT anyway (e.g., obvious ENE), definitive chemoRT is often preferred.

front: In locally advanced larynx cancer, what decides between organ preservation and total laryngectomy?
back: Whether the larynx still works. A functional larynx gets concurrent chemoradiation; a destroyed larynx (cartilage destruction/T4a, non-functional airway or swallow) gets total laryngectomy.
extra: RTOG 91-11: concurrent chemoRT gave the best larynx preservation with similar overall survival.

front: How is nasopharyngeal carcinoma treated, and what role does surgery play?
back: Radiation: RT alone for T1N0 and chemoradiation (often after induction chemo) for nearly everyone else. Surgery is only for salvage.
extra: The skull base makes resection impractical. The neck, including level V and retropharyngeal nodes, is always treated.

front: Which late toxicity does parotid-sparing IMRT reduce?
back: Xerostomia (dry mouth)
extra: PARSPORT showed much less xerostomia with parotid-sparing IMRT than with older conventional RT, without worse tumor control. Dry mouth also drives dental decay and osteoradionecrosis risk.

front: What is the dominant acute toxicity of head and neck chemoradiation, and when does it peak?
back: Mucositis with painful swallowing and weight loss (plus skin reaction); it builds from about weeks 2-3 and peaks near the end of treatment or shortly after.
extra: Managed with pain control, nutrition support (sometimes a feeding tube), and oral care. Taste loss and thick saliva are also common.

front: Dose to which structure is most linked to long-term dysphagia after head and neck RT?
back: The pharyngeal constrictors
extra: Parallel links to know: parotids drive xerostomia, the mandible drives osteoradionecrosis risk.

front: Why is the neck dissected in oral cavity cancer even when it looks clinically negative?
back: Occult nodes are common once the tumor is more than a few millimeters deep. The Tata Memorial trial showed elective neck dissection improved survival over watching the neck.
extra: Sentinel node biopsy is an option for selected early tumors.

front: What did RTOG 9501 and EORTC 22931 show?
back: Adding cisplatin to postoperative RT helped high-risk patients, and the pooled analysis found a consistent benefit only for ENE and/or positive margins.
extra: Other adverse features (PNI, LVSI, pT3-T4, pN2-3, close margins) get postoperative RT alone.

front: What did RTOG 1016 and De-ESCALaTE show for HPV-positive oropharynx cancer?
back: Swapping cisplatin for cetuximab gave worse survival and more recurrences, without meaningfully less toxicity.
extra: This is why HPV-positive disease is not de-escalated off trial.

front: What did the VA Larynx trial and RTOG 91-11 show?
back: VA Larynx: induction chemo then RT matched laryngectomy for survival, and about two-thirds kept their larynx. RTOG 91-11: concurrent cisplatin-RT gave the best larynx preservation, with similar overall survival.
extra: A preserved larynx that cannot protect the airway or allow swallowing is not a success.

front: How is early (T1-T2 N0) glottic cancer treated?
back: Definitive RT to the larynx alone (no elective neck) or transoral larynx-preserving surgery
extra: Early supraglottic cancer instead needs both sides of the neck treated.

front: How is a T4a larynx cancer treated?
back: Total laryngectomy with neck dissection, then postoperative RT or chemoradiation
extra: Chemoradiation is reserved for selected patients who decline surgery.

front: What did PARSPORT show?
back: Parotid-sparing IMRT caused much less xerostomia than conventional RT, without worse tumor control.
extra: The submandibular glands also make saliva, especially at rest.

front: Which thyroid test is followed after neck radiation, and why?
back: TSH, because hypothyroidism is a common late effect of neck radiation
extra: Other late effects include xerostomia, dysphagia, trismus, fibrosis, dental caries, and hearing loss (especially with cisplatin).
